title.narrative: Strengthened Accountability Program II: Diakonia Zambia

description.narrative:
Diakonia arbetar i Zambia med att stärka medborgares förståelse för deras roll i, och hur de kan bidra till, den politiska, ekonomiska och sociala utvecklingen i landet. Diakonia arbetar också för att öka förståelsen för vikten av jämställdhet och jämlikhet, samt att öka kvinnors deltagande i beslutsfattande.
Under de senaste åren har Diakonia implementerat SAP-I programmet (finansierat av Sida), vars syfte har varit att se till att medborgare får ökad tillgång till resurser. Diakonia föreslår nu att implementera en andra fas av projektet; SAP-II. Det nya programmet kommer att bygga på lärdomar av vad som fungerade/fungerade mindre bra under SAP-I, och en uppdaterad kontextanalys av Zambia. Diakonia ansöker om finansiering från Sida till ett värde av SEK 41 400 000 för perioden 2018–2021, för att implementera SAP-II. Ambassaden har allokerat SEK 1 000 000 för att genomföra en oberoende utvärdering vid programmets slut (2021).
SAP-II kommer att täcka ett större geografiskt område än SAP-I. Programmet kommer också att dubbla antalet samarbetspartner (från fem tio). Syftet är fortsatt att bidra till att medborgare för ökade möjligheter att påverka beslutsfattande, kräva transparens och ansvarsutkrävande, och bidra till en mer rättvis naturresursallokering. Diakonias långsiktiga mål med programmet är att förbättra livskvalitén för samhällen (framförallt för kvinnor, ungdomar, fattiga och mest utsatta) i naturresursrika områden i Zambia.

Diakonia is an international development organization made of two Swedish churches. The head office is located in Sweden. In Zambia, Diakonia works to increase Rights Holders (RHs) understanding of their role in political, social and economic development processes, the importance of achieving gender equality and increasing women’s participation.
Over the past years, Diakonia has been implementing their SAP-I programme (supported by the Embassy of Sweden) aimed to ensure that Right Holders (RHs) have increased access to resources through engagement with corporate and public sectors. Diakonia now proposes to implement the SAP-Phase II (SAP-II) based on the achievements, lessons learned, best practices from the SAP-I and the current context in Zambia. Hence, Diakonia has applied to Sida for funding of SEK 41,400,000 for the period 2018-2021 to implement the SAP-II. The Embassy has also allocated a SEK1,000,000.00 for an independent end of program evaluation to be undertaken in 2021.
The SAP-II will see the expansion of the programme to new geographical areas while also scaling up coverage in additional sites in the previous targeted districts. The programme will continue to address challenges of vulnerable communities in predominantly rural areas by strengthening RHs participation in enhancing equality, transparency and accountability in national resource allocation. Diakonia´s overall goal and expected long-term change with the SAP-II is to improve quality of life of communities (especially, women, youth, the poor and most vulnerable groups) in natural resource rich, rural and peri-urban areas of Zambia. The overall programme objective is to empower RHs to hold duty bearers accountable for equitable access and distribution of national resources.

The evaluation found the program valuable, focusing on human rights, gender, amplifying rights holders voices, and environmental issues in mineral rich rural areas. It noted the unique project approach with evidence of coherence among partners and stakeholders. The program broadened the resource base, involving the private sector in community development and promoting sustainable mining practices. Implementing partners' advocacy led to infrastructure development (roads in Solowezi, schools, clinics funded by the mines in collaboration with local authorities), economic empowerment, job creation, and improved service delivery, benefiting vulnerable rural communities. SAP II empowered right holders to demand accountability, fostering a democratic culture across 13 districts and influencing national policy on sustainable mining. Additionally, the program contributed to Zambia's national baseline on Business and Human Rights, supporting the development of a National Action Plan for enhanced implementation of the UN guiding principals on Business and Human Rights. The project aligned with national development plans, government priorities, community needs, and Diakonia's mission of enhancing dignity for poor people.
The following are specific examples of results attained during the implementation period:
Gender Equity and Equality (GEE):Women took on leadership roles in community structures like the Ward Development Committee, leading to increased school enrollment and reduced early marriages. The program addressed cultural barriers to girls' advancement and women's inclusion in household decisions, including abolishing harmful traditions like "Masambilisha" (the celebration of a young boy who impregnants a young girl) in Nyakulenga Chiefdom by HRH Chieftainess Nyakulenga. Traditional leaders, like Senior Chief Kanongesha of the Lunda people of Mwinilunga, promoted gender equality. Networking improved referral pathways for women's rights violations. Gender awareness training by NGOs and Women for Change reached over 3600 individuals, forming 85 awareness groups in Southern Province. Community radio broadcasts on gender reached 100 000 people, disseminating information on women's land ownership. Additionally, women, men, and youth were empowered in income generating activities like village banking, beekeeping, goat farming, and green charcoal production, with some accessing initiatives through the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) and mining companies.
Equitable access to and distribution of natural resources: SAP II, the largest non-state actor initiative in natural resource governance, focused on remote and vulnerable rural areas with rich natural resources. It improved engagements between Rights Holders and Duty Bearers, resulting in tangible actions such as a dental unit in Zimba District, mining activity suspension at Kasenseli Gold Mine, clinic construction in Kalumbila by Lumwana mine, an agriculture officer assigned in Zimba, and electricity in Chikanta of Kalomo. Duty Bearers involved Right Holders in local planning and budgeting, while groups like Policy Dialogue Teams monitored Constituency Development Funds (CDF) funded projects with local authorities. Mining companies collaborated with CSOs on accountability initiatives and CSR through Memorandums of Understanding. Awareness was raised in Nyanja, enhancing participation and rights claiming ability. Trainings and public sensitizations empowered Right Holders to demand equitable services.
Social and environmental accountability: Policy briefs, advocacy for private sector compliance with environmental standards, forest restoration, research on artisanal mining, and conflict mediation between communities and mining companies led to increased private sector commitment to community needs and environmental concerns. This resulted in significant revenue growth, allowing the Solowezi district Council to purchase a grader for road maintenance and begin infrastructure development. Lumwana mine compensated 90% of affected communities in Kalumbila, while Kasanshi mine provided employment through women's jewelry design training and supported conservation farming.
Partner organizations' capacity development: During implementation, Diakonia supported both resource and implementing partners by strengthening governance structures and financial management systems. This included developing governance tools, enhancing compliance with Diakonia requirements through software procurement and onsite training, and providing technical assistance for statutory payments and Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) training. The Embassy's assessment is that the program achieved its goals. Unexpected outcomes included CSOs playing a conflict mediation role, employment creation through skills training and job linkages by Kansashi mines, and the establishment of the annual Zambia Mining Indaba, initially started and financed by the program and now funded by the Zambia Chamber of Mines.
The project has catalysed an accountability culture and sustainable mining practices in the target communities. The community groups formed continue to be human rights advocates and empowered to demand for improved service delivery in their localities.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
